name: printf
plain: `printf` prints text exactly as you describe it, using a format string like in the C language. Unlike echo it does not add a newline unless you ask, and it treats backslash escapes the same way everywhere.
That makes it the right tool for exact output: no trailing newline, a precise hex byte, a padded number, a repeated pattern.
when: Print exact bytes (shellcode, a magic header).
Hash a string with no newline.
Write the same pattern many times.

examples.title: Print with a newline
examples.explain: printf adds nothing for you: write \n where you want a new line.

examples.title: Hash without a newline
examples.explain: Reliable in every shell, unlike echo -n.

examples.title: Insert values
examples.explain: %s is a string, %d a number. The values follow the format.

examples.title: Write raw bytes
examples.explain: \xHH writes one byte. This is how you build tiny test files and payloads.

examples.title: Repeat a pattern
examples.explain: Prints 32 A characters: the format has one %.0s that eats a number but prints nothing, while A is printed each time.

examples.title: Store in a variable
examples.explain: -v (bash) saves the result in a variable instead of printing.

options.plain: The pattern: ordinary text, escapes and % conversions. Reused if more arguments than conversions remain.
String / string with backslash escapes interpreted.
Quote the argument so it can be reused as shell input (bash).
Newline, tab, carriage return, backslash, bell, octal byte, hex byte.
bash builtin: assign the output to VAR.

mistakes: Passing user text as the format: printf "$input" interprets % and backslashes; use printf '%s' "$input".
Using %d with a non-number: you get 0 and a warning.
Forgetting that format is reused for extra arguments.
try: Print your name and a number with %s and %d.
